title: The Most Important Technology in My Classroom
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: In a lightly tongue-in-cheek piece, Stuart declares the spiral notebook — not any app or device — the most important technology in his classroom, citing its total reliability (no charging, no logins, no passwords, immune to ChatGPT) against $1.50-apiece cost. He runs through the everyday tasks the notebooks quietly enable: elaboration writing, vocabulary capture, note-taking, impromptu low-stakes quizzes, and memorization drills — the "spirachis," as his class calls them. The real point beneath the humor is that the notebook itself isn't what makes the learning powerful; it's a delivery vehicle for ten cognitive-science principles (learning is hard, working memory is finite, elaboration deepens understanding, and so on) that Stuart says undergird every instructional decision he makes. He uses the piece to preview his forthcoming Principles of Learning Course, framing the notebook anecdote as proof that sound pedagogy doesn't require expensive or novel technology to work.
points: Stuart deliberately picks the lowest-tech possible tool (a $1.50 notebook) to make a point about ed-tech: reliability and cognitive-science grounding matter more than novelty or digital sophistication.

The notebook is framed as a delivery vehicle, not the source of learning power — the actual power comes from the ten cognitive-science principles (elaboration, retrieval, working memory limits) the notebook tasks are designed around.

Everyday low-stakes uses (impromptu quizzes, vocabulary capture, note-taking) are listed as the notebook's real value, positioning consistent small-grain retrieval opportunities over occasional big digital projects.

The piece implicitly pushes back on assumptions that classroom modernization requires new hardware or apps, arguing instead that principled use of the simplest tools can carry the cognitive-science load.
quotes: There's no question about the most useful technological marvel that my students and I use to grow in mastery of my discipline: the spiral notebook. These little 70-page beauties can be had for $1.50 at our local grocery store.
They require no charging. I've never had a student complain of a log-in issue. No one forgets their password. They've yet to be disrupted by ChatGPT.

If it seems like I'm being a little silly, there is a little bit of that going on here. But a big part of that silliness comes from the joy I have at knowing that these simple tools form the logistical backbone of the work of learning I facilitate in my room each day.

But that learning isn't powerful just because it's happening in spiral notebooks. It's powerful because it's informed by 10 key principles of learning that I've taken away from cognitive science over the years.
And yet, they absolutely undergird each decision I make in my classroom — including my decision to lean so heavily on high-tech solutions like spiral notebooks.
I don't lead in-person workshops on these topics. I don't have any books on them. I've written about them here and there on the blog, but never in an organized or deep manner.
